name: Sorting Problem Again
description: You have an array $$$a$$$ of $$$n$$$ elements. There are also $$$q$$$ modifications of the array. Before the first modification and after each modification, you would like to know the following: What is the minimum length subarray that needs to be sorted in non-decreasing order in order for the array $$$a$$$ to be completely sorted in non-decreasing order? More formally, you want to select a subarray of the array $$$(l, r)$$$ with the minimum value of $$$r - l + 1$$$. After that, you will sort the elements $$$a_{l}, a_{l + 1}, \ldots, a_{r}$$$ and want the condition $$$a_{i} \le a_{i + 1}$$$ to hold for all $$$1 \le i \lt n$$$. If the array is already sorted in non-decreasing order, then $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ should be considered as equal to $$$-1$$$. Note that finding such $$$(l, r)$$$ does not change the array in any way. The modifications themselves take the form: assign $$$a_{pos} = x$$$ for given $$$pos$$$ and $$$x$$$.
input_specification: Each test consists of several test cases. The first line contains an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10$$$) — the number of test cases. Then follows the description of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^{5}$$$). The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_{i}$$$ ($$$0 \le |a_{i}| \le 10^{9}$$$) — the initial elements of the array $$$a$$$. The third line of each test case contains a number $$$q$$$ ($$$0 \le q \le 5 \cdot 10^{5}$$$) — the number of modifications to the array. The following $$$q$$$ lines of each test case contain two integers $$$pos_{i}$$$ ($$$1 \le pos_{i} \le n$$$) and $$$val_{i}$$$ ($$$0 \le |val_{i}| \le 10^{9}$$$) — this means that for the $$$i$$$-th modification, $$$a_{pos_{i}}$$$ is assigned the value $$$val_{i}$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ and the sum of $$$q$$$ for all test cases does not exceed $$$5 \cdot 10^{5}$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output $$$q + 1$$$ lines. Each line should contain $$$2$$$ integers $$$l, r$$$ — the boundaries of the minimum subarray, such that sorting it will make the array $$$a$$$ completely sorted. If $$$a$$$ is already sorted, then output $$$l = -1$$$, $$$r = -1$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1982F — Sorting Problem Again [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
